French troops on patrol with the Afghan army as part of the NATO mission in Afghanistan. The National Assembly voted in favor of Sarkozy's plan, 329-238. The move did not technically require parliamentary approval, but the president's party scheduled the debate to give opponents a chance to voice their opinions -- and to show a majority backed it. Asking the National Assembly to vote on the issue also showed how sensitive the matter is in France. "To cooperate is to lose your independence," French President Charles de Gaulle said at the time. Rejoining NATO's military command, he argued, will give France a seat at the table for decision-making. From its earliest years, the organization's trans-Atlantic ties were strained because U.S. analysts warned that if the European allies failed to increase their contributions to the alliance, they risked losing the support of the United States, according to NATO. Meanwhile, the European nations felt the United States was trying to dominate the organization, according to NATO. De Gaulle's 1966 decision meant no French forces could be under permanent allied command and that France would have no participation in defense planning. In 1995, France rejoined NATO's military committee, which advises NATO's political authorities on military policy and strategy and provides guidance on military matters to NATO's strategic commanders. While France was still not a part of the military command, it contributed troops and funding to NATO activities, including actions in Kosovo and Afghanistan. Half of all French troops outside the country are assigned to NATO military operations. Opponents of Sarkozy's move -- who include some members of his party -- believe de Gaulle, not Sarkozy, had it right. They started a last-minute petition drive to stop his march back into NATO. "With this decision, France will return as a subordinate country and will lose its ability to represent another image in the world," said Nicolas Dupont-Aignan, a member of the French National Assembly. The president's allies calculate Sarkozy's move will strengthen Europe's hand on defense issues. "There will be more European weight in the way decisions will be made," said Louis Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the National Assembly's U.S. Friendship Committee. "Therefore, the balance of power between the USA and Europe will be re-established within this French move." CNN's Sunaina Karkarey and Jim Bittermann contributed to this report .

**PARIS, France (CNN)** — France’s National Assembly voted Tuesday to support President Nicolas Sarkozy’s decision to bring the country back into NATO’s integrated military command, reversing a landmark policy established more than four decades ago by Charles de Gaulle.

The vote gave parliamentary backing to Sarkozy’s plan to restore France to a central role in the alliance’s military planning structure, a move the president has argued will strengthen France’s influence within NATO while preserving its independent nuclear deterrent and sovereign decision-making.

France remained a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization after de Gaulle’s 1966 decision, but withdrew from the alliance’s integrated military command in protest of what he saw as excessive U.S. dominance. The move forced NATO headquarters and allied forces to leave French territory and became a defining symbol of France’s independent foreign policy during the Cold War.

Sarkozy has said that era has passed and that France can better shape NATO from within. His government has argued the return would allow French officers to take senior command posts and give Paris more weight in alliance decisions, particularly as NATO faces missions beyond Europe, including Afghanistan.

Opposition parties sharply criticized the move, accusing Sarkozy of aligning France too closely with Washington and weakening a pillar of French strategic independence.

Socialist and Communist lawmakers argued that rejoining the command structure would dilute France’s distinctive diplomatic voice and make it harder for Paris to resist U.S.-led military initiatives. Critics also objected to the government tying the NATO question to a broader confidence vote, saying the issue deserved a separate national debate.

The government dismissed those concerns, insisting that France would not surrender control over its forces. Officials emphasized that any deployment of French troops would still require a national decision and that France’s nuclear arsenal would remain outside NATO command.

The vote marked one of Sarkozy’s most significant foreign-policy shifts since taking office. It also underscored a broader effort to repair relations with the United States after tensions over the 2003 Iraq war, while presenting France as a more assertive actor inside Western security institutions.

France is expected to formalize its full return to NATO’s integrated military command at the alliance summit marking NATO’s 60th anniversary.

**PARIS — Sarkozy Returns France to NATO’s Military Command After Four Decades Outside**

France formally moved to rejoin NATO’s integrated military command structure this week, ending a policy of strategic distance launched by Charles de Gaulle more than 40 years ago and marking one of the most significant shifts in French defense policy since the Cold War.

President Nicolas Sarkozy’s government secured parliamentary backing in Paris for the decision, arguing that France could better defend its interests by exercising influence inside NATO’s command system rather than standing apart from it. The move returns France to the heart of alliance military planning, while preserving what Sarkozy insists is the country’s independent nuclear deterrent and freedom to decide when and where to deploy French forces.

“France is not surrendering its independence; it is strengthening its influence,” lawmakers from Sarkozy’s center-right majority argued during debate in the National Assembly. Supporters said the old arrangement had become increasingly symbolic, noting that French troops have long served in NATO-led operations in the Balkans, Afghanistan and elsewhere.

Opposition lawmakers denounced the decision as an unnecessary concession to Washington and a break with France’s Gaullist tradition of military autonomy.

“This is not a technical adjustment; it is a political choice,” one Socialist deputy said in the chamber. “It risks aligning France more closely with American strategy at the very moment when Europe should be building its own defense identity.”

Another opposition lawmaker accused the government of “turning the page on a central element of French independence without a referendum and without a real national debate.”

The government survived the parliamentary test, with the National Assembly voting in favor after Prime Minister François Fillon tied the issue to a confidence motion. The vote gave Sarkozy the domestic political authority to announce France’s full return to NATO’s command structure at the alliance summit marking NATO’s 60th anniversary.

## A Gaullist Legacy Reversed

France was a founding member of NATO in 1949, but its relationship with the alliance has long been more complicated than that of most other Western members.

In 1966, President Charles de Gaulle withdrew France from NATO’s integrated military command, saying French forces should not be automatically subordinated to a command structure dominated by the United States. De Gaulle also ordered NATO headquarters and foreign troops stationed under NATO command to leave French territory. NATO’s political headquarters subsequently moved from Paris to Brussels.

France did not leave NATO itself. It remained a member of the Atlantic Alliance, continued to participate in political consultations, and maintained its commitment to collective defense under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. But for decades, Paris stayed outside the alliance’s permanent military command arrangements.

The policy became a symbol of French strategic independence — a way of affirming that France was part of the Western alliance but not simply another follower of U.S. military policy. It also reflected France’s desire to maintain its own nuclear deterrent, known as the *force de frappe*, and to promote Europe as an independent strategic actor.

Yet over time, the practical distance narrowed. French officers took part in NATO missions, French forces operated alongside allied troops, and Paris gradually re-engaged with NATO planning after the Cold War. France participated in NATO-led operations in Bosnia, Kosovo and Afghanistan, often with substantial troop contributions.

Sarkozy and his allies argued that the old posture had become outdated.

“France was already taking part in NATO operations,” a pro-government lawmaker said. “The difference is that now France will also take part in the decisions that shape them.”

## Sarkozy’s Atlantic Turn

Sarkozy has made no secret of his desire to repair and deepen France’s relationship with the United States and NATO after years of tension, particularly over the Iraq War. His government insists that full participation in NATO’s command structure will give French officers senior posts and a greater role in shaping alliance strategy.

French officials have emphasized that the return does not place French nuclear forces under NATO authority and does not require France to send troops automatically into any NATO operation. Deployments will remain subject to national decision-making.

The Élysée Palace has presented the move as compatible with European defense ambitions, arguing that France can strengthen the European Union’s security role while also playing a larger part in NATO.

Critics are unconvinced. Many on the left, as well as some Gaullists, argue that France’s unique voice in world affairs was strengthened by its semi-detached position. They say reintegration risks blurring the distinction between French foreign policy and U.S.-led alliance priorities.

“This decision weakens the message France has carried for decades: that allies can be loyal without being subordinate,” an opposition deputy said.

## NATO Welcomes the Decision

NATO officials and allied governments have welcomed the French move, seeing it as a major step toward alliance cohesion. France is one of Europe’s largest military powers, with nuclear weapons, a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, and significant expeditionary capabilities.

Full reintegration is expected to give France posts within NATO’s military command hierarchy, including senior responsibilities in allied transformation and operational planning. For NATO, France’s return helps close a historic divide inside the alliance at a time when it faces pressure in Afghanistan, questions about relations with Russia, and debates over its future strategic mission.

For Sarkozy, the decision is also meant to recast France’s global role: less defined by symbolic distance from Washington, and more by influence inside the institutions where military decisions are made.

But the controversy in Paris shows that NATO remains more than a defense organization in French political memory. It is a test of sovereignty, identity and France’s place between Europe and the United States.

More than four decades after de Gaulle pulled French forces out of NATO’s military command, Sarkozy has taken France back in — arguing that independence today is not preserved by an empty chair, but by a seat at the table.

The move reflected his broader vision of national sovereignty, strategic independence and an independent French nuclear deterrent.

The president has also said that rejoining the integrated command would not compromise France’s nuclear independence or its freedom to decide whether to deploy troops. French officials have emphasized that France would retain control over its nuclear arsenal and would not automatically commit forces to NATO operations.

The debate has revived a long-running French argument over how to balance national independence, European defense ambitions and transatlantic cooperation. For Sarkozy, full participation in NATO’s military structures is a way to increase French weight within the alliance. For his critics, it marks a symbolic break with the Gaullist policy that kept France at a measured distance from American-led military planning.
